claims.text: Phase stability in nominally equiatomic Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni is principally governed by competition between configurational entropy and local lattice distortions.
Atomic-size mismatches and varying mixing enthalpies cause local lattice distortions in this alloy.
Controlled rapid cooling enhances and retains a high degree of chemical disorder.
Retained chemical disorder inhibits the nucleation and growth of brittle intermetallic phases.
Suppressing brittle intermetallic phases preserves high-temperature strength.
Suppressing brittle intermetallic phases preserves environmental resistance.
Suppressing brittle intermetallic phases preserves radiation tolerance.
Suppressing brittle intermetallic phases preserves cryogenic toughness.
The nominally equiatomic alloy in the proposed initial state has a mixed microstructure.
The proposed initial state contains some local chemical ordering.
Slow cooling after homogenization permits greater chemical ordering than rapid quenching.
The degree and scale of chemical ordering and associated lattice distortions mediate the onset of secondary brittle phases.
Rapid quenching kinetically traps a high-configurational-entropy state and its associated lattice distortions.
Rapid quenching prevents sufficient atomic diffusion to form more stable brittle intermetallic compounds.
A retained disordered, strained solid solution confers balanced mechanical and resistance properties over a broad temperature range.
Relative to slow cooling, rapid quenching will produce a predominantly single-phase disordered microstructure.
Relative to slow cooling, rapid quenching will reduce the amount of incipient intermetallic precipitates.
Relative to rapid quenching, slow cooling will increase local chemical order.
Relative to rapid quenching, slow cooling will promote the early onset of brittle secondary phases.
